piece.caption: AI ad compliance rules for Indian exporters targeting overseas buyers. Pennsylvania has enacted the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, mandating disclosures on any commercial creative significantly generated or altered by AI. Because this applies regardless of where the ad is produced, digital campaigns reaching US audiences must comply. The law specifies that labels must match the media format: a caption disclaimer alone may fail review if the image itself lacks an overlay label. Place clear visual badges directly on synthetic images and videos to keep your ad account clean. Are you already labeling synthetic graphics in your overseas campaigns?

The requirement applies regardless of where an ad was created.
What constitutes significantly modified is subjective, and there are carve-outs for parody, satire, commentary, or evidently fictional content.
The statutory wording targets synthetic content used in a manner creating a false consumer perception about a product or service.

Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
Terrence O'Brien Oct 24, 2026, 6:32 PM UTC Link
Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.
Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.
The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.
The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill , did not immediately return a request for comment.
